newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says U.S. humiliated, Kurdish refugees flee.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says U.S. humiliated, Kurdish refugees flee.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Kurds fled towards Iran on Tuesday as Iraq gloated that the victory of its Kurdish militia allies had restored Baghdad's power over the north and humiliated the United States.

Underlining Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's renewed influence, his government declared an amnesty for Kurds who had lived under Western protection since Baghdad lost control of northern Iraq in 1991.

A television announcement also said Saddam had ordered the resumption of movement of people and goods with the region, ending "all emergency measures which were necessitated by previous extraordinary conditions."

The United States, which last week conducted missile strikes on southern Iraq in reprisal for Iraqi forces fighting alongside their Kurdish allies, had termed the latest fighting a civil war but warned Baghdad and Tehran against becoming involved.

However, the contest appeared already decided when the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) lost their stronghold of Sulaimaniya to the Iraqi-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) on Monday, triggering a flood of refugees towards nearby Iran.

The United Nations said it was preparing for a potential refugee crisis, as up to 75,000 Kurds headed for the Iranian border. Iranian officials, saying the potential number was 200,000, appealed for international aid to cope with the influx.

Refugees streamed to Sairan Ban, one of at least four border points where U.N. officials expected Kurds to gather. With the crossing closed, thousands of people were backed up, hanging out of cars on the hot, dusty road. Tractors pulled wagons piled with belongings.
They were joined by hundreds of armed PUK guerrillas on the run.

Kurds remembered the poison gas Iraq used on villagers in 1988. Iraq again crushed rebellious Kurds in 1991 after its defeat in the Gulf War, prompting the United States and its allies to establish the safe haven in northern Iraq that was supposed to keep Iraqi forces out.
"We're afraid. We don't trust the government of Saddam Hussein," said a headmaster among those fleeing Sulaimaniya, now mostly deserted by its one million or so people.

But witnesses later said that hundreds of Iraqi Kurds were returning from the Iranian border to the homes they had fled, apparently reassured that Iraqi troops were not moving into the city which fell with little fighting.
"There are hundreds of vehicles and perhaps thousands of people," said Stafford Clarry, head of the U.N. relief effort in Sulaimaniya.
"If the border remains closed, if the city remains quiet, then they'll come flocking back," said a senior U.N. official.

Abdullah Mohammed, 45, who makes videocassettes for a living, returned with his wife and seven children on Tuesday, two days after they left, and said: "I left because of Saddam, but Saddam is not there. Just Mr Barzani. He is Kurdish, it's no problem, I'll go home."
Iraq's Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf announced the broad amnesty in Baghdad.
"We have decided to pardon our sons, citizens of the autonomous region under a general and comprehensive amnesty (protecting them) against legal prosecution..."
He said the amnesty covers all but "those who have committed rape, killed state employees and plundered state property".
The Iraqi government was in a celebratory mood after its Kurdish allies stormed to victory despite the U.S. raids last week following the joint Iraqi-KDP capture of the key Kurdish city of Arbil.

"Today, the Iraqi flag flies high and the U.S. flag is only at half mast," the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya said. It described President Bill Clinton as "a caged hyena, rushing around in search of a way out".
Clinton said on Monday Washington was doing its best to help anyone who cooperated with the United States in the Kurdish region to leave.

"America is preparing squadrons of helicopters...to evacuate its fleeing agents, exactly as it did in 1975 in southern Vietnam when it suddenly decided to escape from that country in humiliation," the Iraqi newspaper said.
